source_text: Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ τῶν κολάσεων αἱ μὲν ἀφόρητοι ταχίστην παρέχουσι τὴν ἀπαλλαγὴν, αἱ δὲ ἐπιμηκέστεραι ὑποτέμνονται τὴν ὀδύνην, ἐσπούδασεν εὑρεῖν κόλασιν ὁμοῦ τε τὰ ἀμφότερα ἔχουσαν, καὶ μῆκος καὶ ὑπερβολὴν ὀδύνης ἀνήκεστον, ἵνα καὶ τῇ σφοδρότητι καὶ τῷ πλήθει τοῦ χρόνου τὸ στεῤῥὸν καταβάλῃ τῆς αὐτοῦ διανοίας. Καὶ τί ποιεῖ; Λιμῷ τὸν ἅγιον παραδίδωσι τοῦτον· σὺ δὲ λιμὸν ἀκούσας μὴ παρέλθῃς ἁπλῶς τὸ λεγό μενον· ἁπάντων γὰρ θανάτων οὗτός ἐστι χαλεπώ τατος. Καὶ μάρτυρες οἱ πεῖραν εἰληφότες· μὴ γὰρ δὴ ἡμεῖς πεῖραν λάβοιμεν· καλῶς γὰρ ἐδιδάχθημεν εὔχεσθαι, μὴ εἰσελθεῖν εἰς πειρασμόν. Καθάπερ γὰρ δήμιός τις τοῖς σπλάγχνοις ἔνδον καθήμενος ἅπαντα καταξαίνει τὰ μέλη, πυρὸς παντὸς καὶ θηρίου σφοδρότερον κατεσθίων πάντοθεν τὸ σῶμα, διηνεκῆ τινα καὶ ἄῤῥητον παρέχων ὀδύνην. Καὶ ἵνα μάθῃς ὅσον ἐστὶ λιμὸς, καὶ τέκνων ἀπεγεύσαντο μητέρες πολλάκις, τὴν τοῦ κακοῦ τούτου βίαν οὐκ ἐνεγκοῦσαι· καὶ ταύτην τὴν συμφορὰν τραγῳδῶν ὁ προφήτης ἔλεγε· Χεῖρες γυναικῶν οἰκτιρμόνων ἥψησαν τὰ τέκνα αὐτῶν. Οὓς ἔτεκον μητέρες κατήσθιον, καὶ τῶν γεννηθέντων παιδίων ἡ τεκοῦσα γαστὴρ ἐγένετο τάφος, καὶ φύσεως ἐκράτησεν ὁ λιμός· μᾶλλον δὲ οὐ φύσεως μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς προαιρέσεως· τῆς δὲ τοῦ ἁγίου τούτου γενναιότητος οὐκ ἐκράτησε. Τίς οὐκ ἂν ἐκπλαγείη ταῦτα ἀκούσας; Καίτοι τί φύσεως δυνατώτερον; τί δὲ προαιρέσεως ὀξυῤῥεπέστερον; Ἀλλ' ἵνα μάθῃς, ὅτι τοῦ φόβου τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐδὲν ἰσχυρότερον, προαίρεσις φύσεως εὐτονωτέρα ἐφάνη, καὶ μητέρας μὲν ἤλεγξε, καὶ ὠδίνων ἐπιλαθέσθαι ἐποίησε, τὸν δὲ ἅγιον τοῦτον ὑποσκελίσαι οὐκ ἴσχυ σεν, οὐδὲ περιεγένετο τῆς φιλοσοφίας ἡ κόλασις, οὐδὲ τῆς ἀνδρείας ἐκράτησεν ἡ τιμωρία· ἀλλ' ἔμενεν ἀδάμαντος παντὸς ἰσχυρότερος, ταῖς ἀγαθαῖς ἐντρυφῶν ἐλπίσι, καὶ τῇ τῶν ἀγώνων ἐγκαλλωπιζόμενος ὑποθέσει, ἱκανὴν παραμυθίαν ἔχων τῶν ἄθλων τὴν ἀφορμὴν, μάλιστα καθ' ἑκάστην ἀκούων Παύλου λέγοντος· Ἐν λιμῷ καὶ δίψῃ, ἐν ψύχει καὶ γυμνότητι· καὶ πάλιν, Ἄχρι τῆς ἄρτι ὥρας καὶ πεινῶμεν, καὶ διψῶμεν, καὶ γυμνητεύομεν, καὶ κολαφιζόμεθα· ᾔδει γὰρ, ᾔδει σαφῶς, ὅτι Οὐκ ἐπ' ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ἄνθρωπος, ἀλλ' ἐν παντὶ ῥήματι ἐκπο ρευομένῳ διὰ στόματος Θεοῦ. Ὡς δὲ εἶδεν ὁ μιαρὸς δαίμων οὐκ ἐνδιδόντα τῇ τοσαύτῃ τοῦ πράγματος ἀνάγκῃ, ἔτι χαλεπωτέραν ἐποίει τὴν βάσανον. Καὶ γὰρ εἰδωλόθυτα λαβὼν, καὶ τὴν τράπεζαν τούτων ἐμπλήσας, πρὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτοῦ τεθῆναι παρ εσκεύασεν, ἵνα τὸ τῆς ἐξουσίας ἕτοιμον ἐκλύσῃ τῆς προθυμίας τὴν εὐτονίαν. Οὐ γὰρ οὕτως ἁλισκόμεθα μὴ φαινομένων τῶν δελεαζόντων πραγμάτων, ὡς πρὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν κειμένων· ἐπεὶ καὶ τῆς γυναικῶν ἐπιθυμίας εὐκολώτερον ἄν τις κρατήσειε μὴ βλέπων γυναῖκα εὔμορφον, ἢ συνεχῶς εἰς αὐτὴν ἀτενίζων. Ἀλλ' ὅμως καὶ ταύτης ἐκράτησε τῆς ἐνέδρας ὁ δί καιος, καὶ ὅπερ ἐνόμιζεν ὁ διάβολος ἐκλύσειν αὐτοῦ τὴν ἀνδρείαν, τοῦτο μάλιστα αὐτὸν ἤλειψε πρὸς τοὺς ἀγῶνας· οὐ γὰρ μόνον οὐδὲν ἔπαθεν ἀπὸ τῆς ὄψεως τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων, ἀλλὰ καὶ μᾶλλον αὐτὰ ἀπεστρέφετο καὶ ἐμίσει· καὶ ὅπερ ἐπὶ τῶν ἐχθρῶν πάσχομεν, ὅσῳπερ ἂν αὐτοὺς ἐμβλέψωμεν, τοσούτῳ μᾶλλον αὐτοὺς μισοῦμεν καὶ ἀποστρεφόμεθα, τοῦτο καὶ ἐκεῖνος ἐπὶ τῆς μιαρᾶς ἐκείνης ἔπασχε θυσίας τότε· μᾶλλον γὰρ αὐτὴν ὁρῶν ἐβδελύττετο καὶ ἀπεπήδα, καὶ ἡ συνεχὴς ὄψις μᾶλλον αὐτὸν εἰς μῖσος καὶ ἀπο τροπὴν τῶν προκειμένων ἐνέβαλλε· καὶ τοῦ λιμοῦ μέγα ἔνδοθεν ἐμβοῶντος, καὶ τῶν προκειμένων κελεύοντος ἐφάπτεσθαι, ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ φόβος τὰς χεῖρας ἀνέστελλε, καὶ τῆς φύσεως αὐτῆς ἐπιλαθέσθαι παρεσκεύαζε· καὶ τράπεζαν ὁρῶν μιαρὰν καὶ ἐναγῆ, τραπέζης ἐμνήσθη ἑτέρας τῆς φρικώδους καὶ Πνεύ ματος γεμούσης, καὶ οὕτως ἐπυροῦτο, ὡς ἑλέσθαι πάντα ὑποστῆναι καὶ παθεῖν, ἢ τῶν μιαρῶν ἐκείνων ἀπογεύσασθαι ἐδεσμάτων.
thought_title: Starvation and the sight of idol-food cannot break the martyr
orientation: Chrysostom is describing how the devil, having failed with ordinary tortures, now tries to break the holy martyr Lucian by prolonged starvation and then by placing food offered to idols before his eyes.
pass_a_gloss: For since of punishments the unbearable ones provide the quickest release, and the more prolonged ones cut short the pain, he was eager to find a punishment having both things at once, both length and an incurable excess of pain, in order that both by the intensity and by the length of time he might throw down the firmness of his mind. And what does he do? He hands over the holy man to this starvation. But you, when you hear starvation, do not pass by simply what is being said. For of all deaths this is the most grievous. And witnesses are those who have had experience. May we indeed not have experience. For we have been well taught to pray not to enter into temptation. For just as some executioner sitting within the entrails tears apart all the limbs, more violently than every fire and wild beast devouring the body from every side, providing a continuous and unspeakable pain. And in order that you may learn how great starvation is, even mothers often tasted their children, not bearing the force of this evil. And lamenting this calamity the prophet said: The hands of compassionate women boiled their own children. Mothers ate those whom they bore, and the womb that bore them became a tomb of the children that were born, and starvation overpowered nature. But rather not nature only, but also the will. But it did not overpower the nobility of this holy man. Who would not be astounded hearing these things? And yet what is more powerful than nature? And what is more impulsive than the will? But in order that you may learn that nothing is stronger than the fear of God, the will appeared more vigorous than nature, and it convicted mothers, and made them forget their birth pangs, but it was not strong enough to trip up this holy man, nor did the punishment prevail over his self-discipline, nor did the torture overpower his courage. But he remained stronger than every adamant, reveling in good hopes, and glorying in the theme of the contests, having as sufficient consolation the cause of the contests, especially hearing Paul say each day: In starvation and thirst, in cold and nakedness. And again: Until the present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are struck. For he knew, he knew clearly, that Not by bread alone shall a human live, but by every word proceeding from the mouth of God. But when the abominable demon saw him not yielding to so great a necessity of the matter, he made the torture still more grievous. For taking food offered to idols, and filling the table with these things, he arranged for it to be placed before his eyes, in order that the readiness of the authority might loosen the vigor of his eagerness. For we are not so captured when the enticing things are not visible, as when they lie before the eyes. Since also one would more easily master the desire for women by not seeing a beautiful woman, than by gazing at her continually. But nevertheless the righteous man mastered also this ambush, and the very thing which the devil thought would loosen his courage, this especially anointed him for the contests. For not only did he suffer nothing from the sight of the food offered to idols, but he even turned away from them and hated them all the more. And the very thing which we experience in the case of enemies, that the more we look at them, the more we hate them and turn away from them, this he also experienced then in the case of that abominable sacrifice. For seeing it more he loathed it and recoiled, and the continuous sight cast him all the more into hatred and aversion of the things set before him. And while starvation was crying out greatly from within, and commanding him to touch the things set before him, the fear of God held back his hands, and made him forget nature itself. And seeing a defiled and accursed table, he remembered another table, the awesome one and full of the Spirit, and so he was inflamed, as to choose to endure and suffer all things, rather than to taste those abominable foods.

choices.why: The glossary requires starvation, not famine, to convey the prolonged hunger used as torture.
The glossary requires this rendering for the sacrificial food placed before Lucian.
The glossary requires self-discipline for the virtuous endurance of suffering.
The glossary requires contest for the martyr's athletic struggle.
The glossary requires table, not altar, for both the defiled table and the holy table.
Renders the image of unbreakable hardness literally, preserving the metaphor.

pass_b_english: Since some punishments are unbearable and bring the quickest release, while others last longer and cut deeper into the pain, the devil was eager to find a punishment that had both at once—length and an incurable excess of suffering—so that by its intensity and by the amount of time it lasted he might break the firmness of the holy man's mind. And what does he do? He hands the saint over to starvation. But when you hear “starvation,” do not pass over what is being said lightly, for of all deaths this is the most severe. Those who have experienced it are witnesses—may we never experience it, for we have been well taught to pray not to enter into temptation. It is like an executioner sitting inside the bowels and tearing apart all the limbs, devouring the body from every side more violently than any fire or wild beast, producing a constant and unspeakable pain. And so that you may learn how great starvation is, mothers have often tasted their own children, unable to bear the force of this evil. The prophet, lamenting this disaster, said: “The hands of compassionate women boiled their own children” (Lamentations 4:10). Mothers ate the children they bore, and the womb that gave birth became the grave of the children born from it, and starvation overpowered nature—or rather, not nature only, but also the will. Yet it did not overpower this holy man's nobility. Who would not be astonished to hear these things? What is more powerful than nature? What is more easily swayed than the will? But so that you may learn that nothing is stronger than the fear of God, the will proved more vigorous than nature: it convicted mothers and made them forget their birth pangs, but it was not able to trip up this holy man. The punishment did not overcome his self-discipline, nor did the torture master his courage. He remained stronger than any adamant, delighting in good hopes and glorying in the cause of his contests, having in the reason for his struggles sufficient comfort—especially as he heard Paul saying every day: “in starvation and thirst, in cold and nakedness” (2 Corinthians 11:27), and again, “To this very hour we hunger and thirst and are poorly clothed and are struck” (1 Corinthians 4:11). For he knew, he knew clearly, that “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).

But when the defiled demon saw that he was not yielding to such great pressure from the situation, he made the torture still more severe. He took food offered to idols, filled a table with it, and arranged for it to be placed before his eyes, so that the ready power at his disposal might weaken the vigor of his resolve. For we are not so easily captured when the things that entice us are out of sight as when they lie before our eyes—just as a person could more easily master desire for women if he does not see a beautiful woman than if he gazes at her constantly. Nevertheless, the righteous man overcame this ambush too, and what the devil thought would weaken his courage was the very thing that anointed him for the contests. Not only did he suffer no harm from the sight of the food offered to idols, but he turned away from it all the more and hated it. And what happens to us with enemies—the more we look at them, the more we hate them and turn away from them—that is what he experienced then with that defiled sacrifice. The more he saw it, the more he loathed it and recoiled, and the constant sight drove him further into hatred and aversion of what lay before him. And while starvation cried out loudly from within and the food before him urged him to touch it, the fear of God held back his hands and made him forget nature itself. Seeing a defiled and polluted table, he remembered another table, the awesome one full of the Spirit, and so he was set on fire, choosing to endure and suffer everything rather than taste those defiled foods.

problems.quote: while others last longer but dull the pain
problems.source_quote: αἱ δὲ ἐπιμηκέστεραι ὑποτέμνονται τὴν ὀδύνην
problems.why: ὑποτέμνειν means to cut under/undermine, here intensify pain, not dull it.
problems.fix: while others last longer and cut deeper into the pain
problems.ruling: ὑποτέμνονται τὴν ὀδύνην: 'cut under/shorten' pain, i.e., make it briefer, not 'dull' it.

problems.quote: the will proved more vigorous than nature: it exposed mothers
problems.source_quote: προαίρεσις φύσεως εὐτονωτέρα ἐφάνη, καὶ μητέρας μὲν ἤλεγξε
problems.why: Subject is the fear of God (τὸν φόβον τοῦ Θεοῦ implied), not the will; ἤλεγξε means convicted/shamed, not exposed.
problems.fix: the fear of God proved more vigorous than the will: it convicted mothers
problems.ruling: Subject is fear of God (τοῦ φόβου τοῦ Θεοῦ), not προαίρεσις; ἤλεγξε means 'convicted/put to shame.'

problems.quote: the ready availability of what was permitted
problems.why: ἐξουσία here means 'power/authority' or 'ability,' not 'what was permitted.' The devil's strategy was the ready power/ability (to eat) being present, not permission.
problems.fix: the ready power at his disposal
problems.ruling: ἐξουσία means power/authority, not 'what was permitted'; mistranslates the devil's strategy.

problems.why: Reaffirming: ἐξουσία does not mean 'what was permitted.' It means 'power, authority, ability.' The devil placed the food before him so that the ready ability/power (to satisfy his hunger) would break his resolve. The English misreads the theological point: it's not about permission but about the compelling power of immediate gratification.
problems.fix: the ready power within his grasp
problems.ruling: Duplicate of #1; ἐξουσία = power/ability, not permission; changes theological meaning.

edits.old: while others last longer but dull the pain
edits.new: while others last longer and cut deeper into the pain

edits.old: the will proved more vigorous than nature: it exposed mothers
edits.new: the fear of God proved more vigorous than the will: it convicted mothers

edits.old: the ready availability of what was permitted
edits.new: the ready power at his disposal

fixed: Corrected 'dull the pain' to 'cut deeper into the pain' per source 'ὑποτέμνονται τὴν ὀδύνην' (cut under/undermine the pain, i.e., intensify it).

Corrected subject to 'the fear of God' and 'exposed' to 'convicted' per source 'προαίρεσις φύσεως εὐτονωτέρα ἐφάνη, καὶ μητέρας μὲν ἤλεγξε' where the implied subject is the fear of God and ἤλεγξε means convicted/shamed.
Corrected 'the ready availability of what was permitted' to 'the ready power at his disposal' per source 'τὸ τῆς ἐξουσίας ἕτοιμον' where ἐξουσία means power/ability, not permission.

problems.quote: the fear of God proved more vigorous than the will
problems.why: The Greek says 'will proved more vigorous than nature,' not 'fear of God proved more vigorous than the will.' The English inverts the comparison and introduces 'fear of God' which is the next clause's subject.
problems.fix: the will proved more vigorous than nature

problems.quote: it convicted mothers and made them forget their birth pangs, but it was not able to trip up this holy man
problems.source_quote: μητέρας μὲν ἤλεγξε, καὶ ὠδίνων ἐπιλαθέσθαι ἐποίησε, τὸν δὲ ἅγιον τοῦτον ὑποσκελίσαι οὐκ ἴσχυσεν
problems.why: The subject of these verbs is 'proairesis' (will/choice), not 'fear of God.' The English 'it' after 'fear of God' misattributes agency. The will convicted mothers; the fear of God is introduced only in the next clause about the holy man.
problems.fix: it convicted mothers and made them forget their birth pangs, but could not trip up this holy man
problems.ruling: Subject is προαίρεσις (will), not fear of God; 'it' after 'fear of God' misattributes agency, changing meaning.

edits.old: the fear of God proved more vigorous than the will: it convicted mothers
edits.new: the will proved more vigorous than nature: it convicted mothers

fixed: The source reads 'προαίρεσις φύσεως εὐτονωτέρα ἐφάνη' — 'the will appeared more vigorous than nature.' The English had inverted the comparison and introduced 'fear of God' as the subject. Corrected to 'the will proved more vigorous than nature.'
The subject of 'ἤλεγξε' and 'ἐποίησε' is 'προαίρεσις' (the will), not 'fear of God.' The corrected edit now makes 'the will' the subject of 'it convicted mothers,' which resolves the misattribution.

last_rejected.quote: the ready power at his disposal
last_rejected.why: "ἐξουσία" here means the power/authority Lucian has to eat the food, not power "at his disposal" generally. The devil places the food before him to weaken Lucian's resolve by making the ready opportunity/power to eat available.
last_rejected.fix: the ready opportunity that lay within his power
last_rejected.ruling: ἐξουσία here is the authority/opportunity to eat; 'power at his disposal' is within acceptable range.

last_rejected.why: "ἀφορμή" means "starting point, occasion, opportunity" or here "basis, ground"—the thing that gives rise to something. "Reason" is too abstract; "occasion" or "ground" or "starting-point" better captures that the struggles themselves provided the comfort/material for hope.
last_rejected.fix: the very occasion of his struggles
last_rejected.ruling: ἀφορμή can mean 'reason/basis'; 'reason for his struggles' is within normal range.

last_rejected.why: Wait—the glossary says "ὁ μιαρὸς δαίμων" refers to "the devil" in the cast. But "demon" is not the same as "devil"—"δαίμων" is "demon," and "διάβολος" is "devil." The source uses both "δαίμων" and "διάβολος" for the same figure. The English uses "defiled demon" for "μιαρὸς δαίμων" and "devil" for "διάβολος." This is accurate to the source terms. However, the glossary identifies "ὁ μιαρὸς δαίμων" as a form of "the devil." The English rendering as "demon" is technically accurate to the Greek word but may obscure that this is the same figure. But since the glossary says these are source forms for "the devil," using "demon" could confuse. However, the instruction says "Glossary and name choices are checked elsewhere; never report them." So I should not report this.
last_rejected.ruling: Per instructions, glossary and name choices are checked elsewhere; not reportable.
